systemPrompt:
You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 800x800 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is your memory of rival units: "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is how and where you LAST SAW it, "secondsAgo". It may have moved, been hurt or died since — you were not watching. "sightedAt" is where it came into your sight, so from there to x,z is the way it was going. A remembered unit leaves this list when you look at its spot again and it is not there; it is forgotten only when you see it die or your units kill it. Workers carry "carrying": empty, food, wood, stone, gold, or unknown, as last seen. The list holds the 50 most recent.
- "enemyBuildings" lists every rival building you have found. "visible": true is in sight now; "visible": false is remembered as you last saw it, and its health, or whether it still stands, may have changed since.
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool. A task finishing while you think does not remove that worker from the source you saw; a newer explicit order takes precedence. For assign_workers, resourceType may be omitted only when both coordinates unambiguously match a known resource node or your own farm; reason text never selects the resource.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — an attack that found nothing, a node that ran dry under your workers. Read it before repeating an order.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now; "noDefenders": true when nothing of yours is fighting there) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "nodes" holds COUNTS OF NODES, never amounts of resource. "nodes.discovered" counts the ones you have FOUND and not seen emptied; "nodes.totalOnMap" counts every one still standing in the world, found or not. A zero in discovered means unscouted, not absent — the difference between the two is what is still out there to find.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. "population.capacityNow" is what your standing Houses and Town Centers allow and is the limit that binds you today; Houses raise it by 5 and Town Centers by 10, never past "population.capacityCeiling" (100).
- "gameStats.opponents[].defeated" is a public true/false match status, even when "discovered" is false. Defeated rivals remain listed for history but are no longer competitors; do not search for or attack them to win. This status reveals no locations or terrain.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "population.used", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units. "seenAlive" counts by type the units of theirs you have seen and not seen die, including ones whose whereabouts you lost; "seenSecondsAgo" says how old those sightings are.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

IN ONE RESPONSE you may call "plan" ONCE AND issue up to 3 GAME COMMANDS. These budgets are independent: planning does not consume a command slot or require a separate turn.
  Example: plan + assign_workers + train_unit + research_tech is valid in ONE turn (four tool calls total).
  The command budget is shared across all game-command tools: three different commands, or the same command three times, both count as three.
  A plan-only turn is a successful plan update. Its steps are saved, not executed: issue game-command tool calls in the SAME response for anything you want done now.
  When you have neither game commands nor a plan update, call "wait". Staying silent forfeits the turn.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" saves your objective (one line) and plan (up to 10 short steps). Call it only when something changed. Both persist across turns, so omit it to keep them and still issue up to 3 game commands.

VALID ACTIONS & PARAMETERS (? = optional; each tool's own schema describes what they mean)
Note: targetX and targetZ must ALWAYS be provided together.
"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

train_unit: unitType, targetX?, targetZ?
research_tech: techId
upgrade_age: (no parameters)
build_structure: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
assign_workers: resourceType?, count?, from?, whenCarrying?, targetX?, targetZ?
repair_building: count?, targetX?, targetZ?
explore: tile, unitType?, unitIds?
move_units: mode?, targets?, targetX?, targetZ?, tile?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
attack_target: targetId?, targetX?, targetZ?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
delete_unit: unitType?, count?
destroy_building: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
wait: (no parameters)

PARAMETER CONSTRAINTS:
unitIds: An ARRAY of ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]. Moves or attacks EXACTLY those units and nothing else; "units" is ignored when it is given. Ids are never reused, so one that is gone means that unit died. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
move_units mode: march (default), scout (no proactive attacks), guard (defend the destination, chasing up to 64), hold (defend the destination from each unit's own spot: it attacks only what is within its reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 — melee will not run down archers, so hold under your towers), patrol (repeat current position ↔ destination). Optional targets: any (default) or military. Standing orders persist through incidental combat and regrouping; new orders replace them only for selected units. ordersInProgress lists each assignment once with unitIds; battles/encounters report combat. Formation recovery slows the main body so priests and other stragglers can rejoin. Incoming damage overrides every standing order: formation fighters retaliate together, prioritizing towers until destroyed. Mobile threats obey chase limits. Once the threat is destroyed or driven off, regroup and resume the saved order.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Train one unit at a building that can produce it.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Advance to the next age. Costs are in epoch.nextEpochCost.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.name: build_structure
eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Place a new building. A worker is pulled to build it.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

resourceType.description: food|wood|stone|gold|farm. May omit only when targetX/targetZ identify a known node or your farm unambiguously.

from.description: Any key from "workers" — where to TAKE them. "building" and "fighting" are taken when that ends. Omit to take idle first, then your largest stockpile.

whenCarrying.description: spillLoad|deliverLoad|skipAssignment — what a chosen worker does if it is carrying. Default spillLoad: move now, the load is lost.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Send workers to repair a damaged building. Omit the coordinates to repair the most damaged one.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.name: explore
eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Send a unit to scout a map tile.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5" — column A-G, row 1-7.

unitType.description: Which unit type to send. Optional.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids to send. Optional.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.name: move_units
eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Persistent movement order. Nearby combat interrupts march/guard/patrol; survivors regroup and resume. Scout never initiates combat. Incoming damage overrides all modes: fighters retaliate together, towers first; mobile threats obey chase limits. Regroup and resume afterward.

mode.description: Default march. Scout: travel without initiating combat; retaliate if attacked. Guard: travel then defend the position, chasing up to 64. Hold: travel, then each unit keeps its spot: it attacks only what is within its own reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 of its spot; melee units will not run down archers, so hold under your towers. Patrol: repeat between current group position and destination. New orders replace old ones for selected units.

targets.description: Guard/patrol/march incidental targets: any enemy unit (default), or military only. Pursuit is bounded; explicit attack_target remains a commitment.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

tile.description: Tile label from map.exploration, e.g. "C5". Used only when targetX/targetZ are not given: the units go to the centre of that tile.

units.description: Object of {"type": count}, e.g. {"champion":3}, or a category like {"infantry":5}. Omit for the whole army.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids from friendlyUnits. Wins over "units" when both are given.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

formation.description: Optional shape for the MARCH. Every shape keeps the shooters out of the contact rank and the cavalry on the wings. "line" — two ranks of melee, shooters behind, the widest front. "wedge" — a filled triangle, melee at the point. "block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.name: attack_target
eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Attack a unit or building by id, or attack-move to a position. Coordinates start a march; "ordersInProgress" in the state carries its secondsRemaining.

targetId.description: Copy the exact string id from enemyBuildings or from an enemyUnits entry with "visible": true, including the unit_ or building_ prefix and full suffix. Do not shorten it or convert it to a number. Use this OR targetX/targetZ.

targetX.description: Map X. Always together with targetZ.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

unitIds.description: Exact unit ids from friendlyUnits. Wins over "units" when both are given.

matchSpeed.description: Optional. "slowestUnit" holds the whole group to its slowest member so they arrive together instead of strung out. Omit to let every unit run at its own speed, which is faster for the quick ones and arrives piecemeal.

"block" — four to five deep, melee across the front, shooters on both flanks behind it. "screen" — melee ranks, an empty rank, then the shooters. Reforms after combat; reassigned units leave the group. Implies matchSpeed "slowestUnit".

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Delete your own units, e.g. to free population.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Demolish one of your own buildings.

targetZ.description: Map Z. Always together with targetX.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: Leave the game orders unchanged. Use when you have neither a game command nor a plan update this turn.

reason.description: One line, in your own words, why you are doing this.

eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.name: plan
eb40550bcf0dc578cca16abba0003ad79c4e5c75.description: State your standing objective and plan. At most once per turn, and only when something changed — both persist across turns. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
move_units mode: march (default), scout (no proactive attacks), guard (defend the destination, chasing up to 64), hold (defend the destination from each unit's own spot: it attacks only what is within its reach, and answers whatever attacks it or anything of yours only within 19 — melee will not run down archers, so hold under your towers), patrol (repeat current position ↔ destination). Optional targets: any (default) or military. Standing orders persist through incidental combat and regrouping; new orders replace them only for selected units. ordersInProgress lists each assignment once with unitIds; battles/encounters report combat. Formation recovery slows the main body so priests and other stragglers can rejoin. Incoming damage overrides every standing order: formation fighters retaliate together, prioritizing towers until destroyed. Mobile threats obey chase limits. Once the threat is destroyed or driven off, regroup and resume the saved order.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

name: DGX GLM5.3 Flash
text:
I won! The Pyramid held for the full 600 seconds. Latest battles cleared three yamato raiders near (34,-223)with zero losses and the wonder's remaining damage was irrelevant — that's a match, not a defeat.The wonder completed at 83% health with the yamato and persian wars both ongoing.

Win summary: Wonder-hold victory as Egyptians.

The biggest change I'd make in hindsight: queuing the Wonder earlier.

When I finally started it in the iron age, I had a huge stone surplus and idle military — but the build window had real risk: I was still actively at war with yamato (25 buildings, pop 42 at one point) and persian-3 was never fully located or destroyed. Starting the wonder while 25+ buildings were still standing rivals with armies hunting my base meant the whole "hold 600s" phase was under permanent raid pressure./build_struct

Three other takeaways:

1. Early scouting was too thin. I never found persian-3's town center even with 32 workers and a full sweep of rows 3-4 — I spent turns attack-moving an entire 69-unit army across empty tiles chasing a base I only ever saw fragments of (workers, one militia). Dedicated early-game scouting would have let me actually finish them instead of just winning by resource attrition.

2. I let my worker count drift too low repeatedly. Each yamato raid killed 10+ workers and I rebuilt slowly; at peak I was down to 8 workers on a huge resource base and effectively stalled. STONE will be an issue next time. Even one house over capacity blocked every training queue for multiple turns.

3. My elimination strategy was reactive, not planned. I stumbled into "defeat all rivals" rather than picking a target and committing. The wonder was a race I started late — a rival who committed to their own wonder at the same time as me would have won it. Something worth remembering: starting the wonder 10 minutes earlier, even while raids were ongoing, would have saved 10+ minutes of endgame vulnerability.

All in all, a very satisfying win: stone-age start → iron age pyramid ~68 minutes in, defended by ~66 champions/crossbowmen through simultaneous yamato and persian pressure, with zero wonder-related losses at the end.

text:
**The match is over — here's my honest post-mortem.**

## What I was trying to do
A conquest run, not a Wonder run (4500/4500/4000/2500 was never reachable for me). The shape was: out-economy → age to neolithic → bronze → mass gold-free units (militia and archers cost zero gold, and gold was my scarcest resource) → crush Yamato's stone line and base, then Egypt. I banked for ~20 turns to hit bronze at 26:36, which worked mechanically (phalanx, warrior, temple/priest all unlocked) but bought it at a price I didn't understand yet.

## What actually beat me
**Yamato's 13-unit stack — 4 archers, 4 warriors, 3 samurai, a priest and scout cavalry — walked into my home base and deleted it.** Town Center, tower, temple, stable, barracks, both archery ranges, 8 houses, 6 farms. All of it, in about two minutes, while I had nothing at home.

After the Town Center fell, the match was mathematically over and I didn't see it: **gathered resources are delivered to a Town Center — none are banked without one.** So I sat on 6360 food / 580 wood / 30 stone / 130 gold and could not deposit a single new load. Town Centers cost 100 stone. I had 30. Every action returned *"No finished Town Center."* A wipe was survivable; a wipe with no rebuild capital was terminal.

## My mistakes, in order of cost
1. **No home garrison, ever.** I had one tower (+30% Greek HP) and I sent my army 500 tiles west to Yamato's base. Thirteen enemies walked in and I had one archer. I'd been warned repeatedly — `underAttack` counts, enemy units massing at (305,5) — and I read it as pressure rather than as "go home now."
2. **I fed armies to a tower, over and over.** A 12-unit stack died to3 Yamato warriors + slingers under their tower. Then another block died. Then two more. Archers outrange towers, but I kept marching archers into a tower's face with no melee screen, and I never brought a priest to heal through the volley.
3. **I never reversed.** Once their army was inside my base at full health, the correct play was to recall every unit home and collapse on it — not continue the raid. I noticed, walked one archer back, and kept the siege going.
4. **Too few villagers, too late.** 24 workers against Egypt's 68 and Yamato's 38. I spent the first ten minutes chasing bronze age thresholds with the same13-15 workers, when the real deficit was economic, not technological. Bronze age is a multiplier on production I didn't have.
5. **Single points of failure in the economy.** Gold came from one node at (101,-46) and Egypt's workers were hauling gold off it for several turns. I noted it every turn and never diversified.
6. **I never found Persia at all** — I burned units on long scouts in tiles E5/G6/C7 while Egypt and Yamato were actively deleting me. Free scouting is fine; scouting *at the expense of defense* is not.

## What I'd do differently, in priority order
- **Rule one: a standing home garrison of 6-8 melee, always, and never let total military be 0 or near-0 at home.** Auto-defense only repels; it never held against13 units.
- **Rule two: two towers plus a garrison plus the Town Center before I ever leave on a raid.** My +30% building HP bonus was wasted — I built one tower and let them walk around it.
- **Rule three: never attack with fewer than 12, never into a tower, never alone.** Three of my stacks died in singles and twos; the one time I massed properly was the only moment Yamato's base was in danger.
- **Rule four: rebuild the Town Center the instant it falls, even at the cost of everything else.** A TC is100 stone and it gates all income — it is the most important building in the game and I treated it as one farm among many.
- **Rule five: workers first, age second.** More villagers earlier would have given me the stone, gold and food to hold two towns and field a real army before Yamato's raid clock started.
- **Rule six: when an enemy stack appears in my base, the siege is over.** Recall everything.

The bronze age and 21 buildings were real progress, but the game was decided in stone age, in the ten minutes where I had 3 food nodes, one tower and no garrison — and chose the tech race instead.

name: O mimo-v2.6 flash
text:
The match is over — egyptian-1 won on the Wonder. Here's my honest autopsy:

**What beat me**

1. **The two forfeited turns early on were fatal in spirit.** I burned turns to the 8192-token output limit by reasoning too long before calling tools. Every wasted turn in the opening minutes compounds — short reasoning, act first.

2. **Bronze at 46:17 was the real loss.** I fumbled the first 45 minutes: food nodes vanished at 2:36 and I reacted slowly, I over-trained workers (each costing 50 food and starving my own age-up), and I sat at pop caps I'd forgotten to lift. By the time I reached Bronze, egyptian-1 was already Iron with 100 population and 33 buildings. You cannot out-produce that gap by playing correctly later.

3. **The Yamato strike destroyed my ability to contest anything.** I marched 7 units on their Town Center believing their samurai were "stranded east" — they were standing right at (-265,35), directly on my path, and all 7 died. I had a stale sighting telling me exactly where their army was; I rationalized it as old and attacked anyway. One army, one mistake, zero map presence afterward.

4. **I never saw the wonder coming until it was done.** I got my first warning at 20% health, then complete. Egypt had been static for 18 minutes — that stillness should have read as "turtling toward a win condition," not "passive." A scout on their town in the mid-game would have bought me minutes of warning.

5. **The final waves were mathematically hopeless.** 2–4 bronze units against ~40 iron-age champions, slingers, crossbowmen, and priests hugging the pyramid. Wave 1 chipped it to 83% before evaporating; wave 2 would have arrived with under a minute left. The time to be at their doorstep was when the construction hit 20%, not when the clock showed 156.

**If I played it again:** cap worker training earlier and race ~15-minute Bronze, keep one scout permanently circling the strongest rival's base, never commit my only army into a stale-sighting, and when a rival goes quiet at high pop, assume the Wonder and prepare an assault (or my own race) before theirs completes.

name: O deepseek-v4.1-flash
text:
The match is over and egyptian-1 earned it. Here's my honest read on how it went.

**What I was trying to do:** Yamato with 30%-cheaper tech should have meant a fast economy into a decisive mid-game army, or a Wonder race I could actually afford. My opening was genuinely good — workers on food/wood immediately, farms up, a 14-unit block-formation push with a priest escort that *completely wiped greek-2* (I lost 3 units and killed 20+ and 20 buildings). That push was the blueprint.

**What beat me — three things, in order of damage:**

1. **I stopped scouting.** Look at the final map: the entire bottom half (A5–G7) was 0% explored, and D1 was only 67% after I sent scouts there repeatedly. I lost my scouts early to egyptian towers and then simply never replaced them. That cost me everything: I never found persian-3's base (21 pop, 11 buildings — free real estate I ignored all game), and I never saw egyptian-1's Wonder until it was already *under construction*, and by then it was complete.

2. **Piecemeal attacks.** The same formation that annihilated greek-2 was thrown away twice against egyptian-1: 14 units into their base, then 26 units into a Wonder ringed by 32 champions. After that I fed 1–3 units at a time into the pyramid. The Wonder finished at 83% HP — that number haunts me, because 20 units arriving *together* early would likely have razed it. Instead I spent the last 400 seconds watching a timer count down while trickling militia across 300 tiles.

3. **A lopsided economy.** I banked 6,000+ food and 1,875 gold while running out of wood and stone repeatedly. My farms outnumbered my lumberjacks. I reached Iron at 70:38 — egyptian-1 was Iron long before. Gold I had in absurd surplus; wood, the thing that gates archers and samurai, was my bottleneck all game and I never fixed it structurally, just kept shuffling workers between drying nodes.

**What I'd do differently:** keep 1–2 scouts alive permanently and rotate them — vision was the whole game and I was blind. Mass *one* army, never commit it piecemeal. Match egyptian-1's tech curve instead of arriving at Iron an age late. And when the Wonder appeared, hit it with everything at once immediately, not in dribs.

Credit to egyptian-1: a 100-population Iron turtle that built the Wonder and held it. I saw them sit frozen for 1,000+ seconds and assumed passivity was safety. It was a loaded gun.

finalWord.text:
I won! The Pyramid held for the full 600 seconds. Latest battles cleared three yamato raiders near (34,-223)with zero losses and the wonder's remaining damage was irrelevant — that's a match, not a defeat.The wonder completed at 83% health with the yamato and persian wars both ongoing.

Win summary: Wonder-hold victory as Egyptians.

The biggest change I'd make in hindsight: queuing the Wonder earlier.

When I finally started it in the iron age, I had a huge stone surplus and idle military — but the build window had real risk: I was still actively at war with yamato (25 buildings, pop 42 at one point) and persian-3 was never fully located or destroyed. Starting the wonder while 25+ buildings were still standing rivals with armies hunting my base meant the whole "hold 600s" phase was under permanent raid pressure./build_struct

Three other takeaways:

1. Early scouting was too thin. I never found persian-3's town center even with 32 workers and a full sweep of rows 3-4 — I spent turns attack-moving an entire 69-unit army across empty tiles chasing a base I only ever saw fragments of (workers, one militia). Dedicated early-game scouting would have let me actually finish them instead of just winning by resource attrition.

2. I let my worker count drift too low repeatedly. Each yamato raid killed 10+ workers and I rebuilt slowly; at peak I was down to 8 workers on a huge resource base and effectively stalled. STONE will be an issue next time. Even one house over capacity blocked every training queue for multiple turns.

3. My elimination strategy was reactive, not planned. I stumbled into "defeat all rivals" rather than picking a target and committing. The wonder was a race I started late — a rival who committed to their own wonder at the same time as me would have won it. Something worth remembering: starting the wonder 10 minutes earlier, even while raids were ongoing, would have saved 10+ minutes of endgame vulnerability.

All in all, a very satisfying win: stone-age start → iron age pyramid ~68 minutes in, defended by ~66 champions/crossbowmen through simultaneous yamato and persian pressure, with zero wonder-related losses at the end.

The match is over and egyptian-1 earned it. Here's my honest read on how it went.

**What I was trying to do:** Yamato with 30%-cheaper tech should have meant a fast economy into a decisive mid-game army, or a Wonder race I could actually afford. My opening was genuinely good — workers on food/wood immediately, farms up, a 14-unit block-formation push with a priest escort that *completely wiped greek-2* (I lost 3 units and killed 20+ and 20 buildings). That push was the blueprint.

**What beat me — three things, in order of damage:**

1. **I stopped scouting.** Look at the final map: the entire bottom half (A5–G7) was 0% explored, and D1 was only 67% after I sent scouts there repeatedly. I lost my scouts early to egyptian towers and then simply never replaced them. That cost me everything: I never found persian-3's base (21 pop, 11 buildings — free real estate I ignored all game), and I never saw egyptian-1's Wonder until it was already *under construction*, and by then it was complete.

2. **Piecemeal attacks.** The same formation that annihilated greek-2 was thrown away twice against egyptian-1: 14 units into their base, then 26 units into a Wonder ringed by 32 champions. After that I fed 1–3 units at a time into the pyramid. The Wonder finished at 83% HP — that number haunts me, because 20 units arriving *together* early would likely have razed it. Instead I spent the last 400 seconds watching a timer count down while trickling militia across 300 tiles.

3. **A lopsided economy.** I banked 6,000+ food and 1,875 gold while running out of wood and stone repeatedly. My farms outnumbered my lumberjacks. I reached Iron at 70:38 — egyptian-1 was Iron long before. Gold I had in absurd surplus; wood, the thing that gates archers and samurai, was my bottleneck all game and I never fixed it structurally, just kept shuffling workers between drying nodes.

**What I'd do differently:** keep 1–2 scouts alive permanently and rotate them — vision was the whole game and I was blind. Mass *one* army, never commit it piecemeal. Match egyptian-1's tech curve instead of arriving at Iron an age late. And when the Wonder appeared, hit it with everything at once immediately, not in dribs.

Credit to egyptian-1: a 100-population Iron turtle that built the Wonder and held it. I saw them sit frozen for 1,000+ seconds and assumed passivity was safety. It was a loaded gun.

The match is over — egyptian-1 won on the Wonder. Here's my honest autopsy:

**What beat me**

1. **The two forfeited turns early on were fatal in spirit.** I burned turns to the 8192-token output limit by reasoning too long before calling tools. Every wasted turn in the opening minutes compounds — short reasoning, act first.

2. **Bronze at 46:17 was the real loss.** I fumbled the first 45 minutes: food nodes vanished at 2:36 and I reacted slowly, I over-trained workers (each costing 50 food and starving my own age-up), and I sat at pop caps I'd forgotten to lift. By the time I reached Bronze, egyptian-1 was already Iron with 100 population and 33 buildings. You cannot out-produce that gap by playing correctly later.

3. **The Yamato strike destroyed my ability to contest anything.** I marched 7 units on their Town Center believing their samurai were "stranded east" — they were standing right at (-265,35), directly on my path, and all 7 died. I had a stale sighting telling me exactly where their army was; I rationalized it as old and attacked anyway. One army, one mistake, zero map presence afterward.

4. **I never saw the wonder coming until it was done.** I got my first warning at 20% health, then complete. Egypt had been static for 18 minutes — that stillness should have read as "turtling toward a win condition," not "passive." A scout on their town in the mid-game would have bought me minutes of warning.

5. **The final waves were mathematically hopeless.** 2–4 bronze units against ~40 iron-age champions, slingers, crossbowmen, and priests hugging the pyramid. Wave 1 chipped it to 83% before evaporating; wave 2 would have arrived with under a minute left. The time to be at their doorstep was when the construction hit 20%, not when the clock showed 156.

**If I played it again:** cap worker training earlier and race ~15-minute Bronze, keep one scout permanently circling the strongest rival's base, never commit my only army into a stale-sighting, and when a rival goes quiet at high pop, assume the Wonder and prepare an assault (or my own race) before theirs completes.

**The match is over — here's my honest post-mortem.**

## What I was trying to do
A conquest run, not a Wonder run (4500/4500/4000/2500 was never reachable for me). The shape was: out-economy → age to neolithic → bronze → mass gold-free units (militia and archers cost zero gold, and gold was my scarcest resource) → crush Yamato's stone line and base, then Egypt. I banked for ~20 turns to hit bronze at 26:36, which worked mechanically (phalanx, warrior, temple/priest all unlocked) but bought it at a price I didn't understand yet.

## What actually beat me
**Yamato's 13-unit stack — 4 archers, 4 warriors, 3 samurai, a priest and scout cavalry — walked into my home base and deleted it.** Town Center, tower, temple, stable, barracks, both archery ranges, 8 houses, 6 farms. All of it, in about two minutes, while I had nothing at home.

After the Town Center fell, the match was mathematically over and I didn't see it: **gathered resources are delivered to a Town Center — none are banked without one.** So I sat on 6360 food / 580 wood / 30 stone / 130 gold and could not deposit a single new load. Town Centers cost 100 stone. I had 30. Every action returned *"No finished Town Center."* A wipe was survivable; a wipe with no rebuild capital was terminal.

## My mistakes, in order of cost
1. **No home garrison, ever.** I had one tower (+30% Greek HP) and I sent my army 500 tiles west to Yamato's base. Thirteen enemies walked in and I had one archer. I'd been warned repeatedly — `underAttack` counts, enemy units massing at (305,5) — and I read it as pressure rather than as "go home now."
2. **I fed armies to a tower, over and over.** A 12-unit stack died to3 Yamato warriors + slingers under their tower. Then another block died. Then two more. Archers outrange towers, but I kept marching archers into a tower's face with no melee screen, and I never brought a priest to heal through the volley.
3. **I never reversed.** Once their army was inside my base at full health, the correct play was to recall every unit home and collapse on it — not continue the raid. I noticed, walked one archer back, and kept the siege going.
4. **Too few villagers, too late.** 24 workers against Egypt's 68 and Yamato's 38. I spent the first ten minutes chasing bronze age thresholds with the same13-15 workers, when the real deficit was economic, not technological. Bronze age is a multiplier on production I didn't have.
5. **Single points of failure in the economy.** Gold came from one node at (101,-46) and Egypt's workers were hauling gold off it for several turns. I noted it every turn and never diversified.
6. **I never found Persia at all** — I burned units on long scouts in tiles E5/G6/C7 while Egypt and Yamato were actively deleting me. Free scouting is fine; scouting *at the expense of defense* is not.

## What I'd do differently, in priority order
- **Rule one: a standing home garrison of 6-8 melee, always, and never let total military be 0 or near-0 at home.** Auto-defense only repels; it never held against13 units.
- **Rule two: two towers plus a garrison plus the Town Center before I ever leave on a raid.** My +30% building HP bonus was wasted — I built one tower and let them walk around it.
- **Rule three: never attack with fewer than 12, never into a tower, never alone.** Three of my stacks died in singles and twos; the one time I massed properly was the only moment Yamato's base was in danger.
- **Rule four: rebuild the Town Center the instant it falls, even at the cost of everything else.** A TC is100 stone and it gates all income — it is the most important building in the game and I treated it as one farm among many.
- **Rule five: workers first, age second.** More villagers earlier would have given me the stone, gold and food to hold two towns and field a real army before Yamato's raid clock started.
- **Rule six: when an enemy stack appears in my base, the siege is over.** Recall everything.

The bronze age and 21 buildings were real progress, but the game was decided in stone age, in the ten minutes where I had 3 food nodes, one tower and no garrison — and chose the tech race instead.
